scenes.heading: Percentage composition and formulas
scenes.sub: What is it made of, and in what proportions?
scenes.say: When chemists make a new substance, one of the first questions is: what is it made of, and in what proportions? Let's find out how they answer it.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A food label shows the fraction of sugar, protein, fat
scenes.science: Percentage composition: fraction of mass from each element
scenes.breaks: Two batches of muesli bars can vary a bit; a pure compound has the same composition every time.
scenes.say: A muesli bar label shows what fraction is sugar, protein and fat, for one bar or a whole box. Percentage composition is what fraction of a compound's mass comes from each element. Water is always eleven point one percent hydrogen, from a drop to a swimming pool.
scenes.caption: A muesli bar label shows what fraction is sugar, protein and fat, for one bar or a whole box. Percentage composition is what fraction of a compound's mass comes from each element. Water is always 11.1% hydrogen, from a drop to a swimming pool.

scenes.heading: Nitrogen in a fertiliser
scenes.question: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃.
scenes.say: Percentage equals part over whole, times one hundred. Ammonium nitrate has two nitrogens, so count every atom! Its molar mass is eighty. The nitrogen mass is twenty-eight. Twenty-eight over eighty, times one hundred, gives thirty-five percent nitrogen.
scenes.caption: Percentage = part ÷ whole × 100. Ammonium nitrate has TWO nitrogens, so count every atom! Its molar mass is 80.0. The nitrogen mass is 28.0. 28.0 ÷ 80.0 × 100 gives 35.0% nitrogen.

scenes.heading: Empirical vs molecular

left.title: Empirical formula
points: Ionic compounds: always this, e.g. MgO

scenes.say: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms, like simplifying a punch recipe. The molecular formula is the actual count in one molecule. Glucose is C six H twelve O six, but its empirical formula is C H two O.
scenes.caption: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms, like simplifying a punch recipe. The molecular formula is the actual count in one molecule. Glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆, but its empirical formula is CH₂O.

scenes.heading: Finding an empirical formula
steps: Mass to moles: divide by Ar
scenes.say: Remember the rhyme: percent to mass, mass to mole, divide by small, times till whole. You must convert to moles, because equal masses of different elements contain different numbers of atoms, like a bag of jelly beans versus marshmallows.

scenes.heading: When the ratio isn't whole
scenes.question: An oxide of iron is 70.0% iron and 30.0% oxygen by mass. Find its empirical formula.
scenes.say: Divide each percentage by the atomic mass: one point two five moles of iron, and one point eight seven five of oxygen. Divide by the smallest: one to one point five. It ends in point five, so multiply by two. It's F E two O three.
scenes.caption: Divide each percentage by the atomic mass: 1.25 mol of iron and 1.875 mol of oxygen. Divide by the smallest: 1 : 1.5. It ends in .5, so multiply by 2. It's Fe₂O₃.

scenes.heading: Empirical to molecular
scenes.say: If you know the molar mass, divide it by the empirical formula mass. For glucose, one hundred and eighty divided by thirty is six. So multiply C H two O by six to get C six H twelve O six.
scenes.caption: If you know the molar mass, divide it by the empirical formula mass. For glucose, 180 ÷ 30.0 = 6. So multiply CH₂O by 6 to get C₆H₁₂O₆.

scenes.say: Quick recap. Percentage is part over whole, times one hundred, and they should add to about one hundred. For empirical formulas: percent to mass, mass to mole, divide by small, times till whole. Now try the practice questions!
